chief_complaint: muffled heart sounds, low blood pressure, and jugular vein swelling
hpi_details: A 56-year-old female presents to the clinic with muffled heart sounds, low blood pressure, and jugular vein swelling. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks her heart is suddenly giving out and backing up fluid into her neck because of poor circulation or weak heart muscles.
concerns: She is worried that her heart might suddenly stop beating while she is alone at home.
expectations: She hopes the doctor can run a heart scan right away and give her medicine to bring her blood pressure back up.

investigation_events.title: Emergency bedside echocardiogram
investigation_events.availability_message: The emergency bedside echocardiogram report is now available.

results.value: Large circumferential pericardial effusion measuring 25 mm with right-atrial systolic and right-ventricular diastolic collapse; plethoric IVC
results.reference_range: No pericardial effusion or chamber collapse

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pericardial Tamponade is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Plan for Pericardial Tamponade: Emergent bedside echocardiogram and ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Pericardial Tamponade.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Tension pneumothorax without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Beck's triad present — treat as an immediate emergency.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.

teaching.one_liner: Fluid accumulating in the pericardial sac compresses the heart, causing Beck's triad — low blood pressure, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck veins — a life-threatening emergency needing urgent pericardiocentesis.
red_flags: Beck's triad present — treat as an immediate emergency

must_ask.say: How quickly did you start feeling this unwell?
Do you feel faint or dizzy?
Have you had any recent illness, trauma, or procedures?

history.answer: I've been feeling terribly short of breath and completely wiped out with fatigue.
It started gradually about four or five days ago, and it has been getting steadily worse every day.
At first it was just when walking, but now I feel breathless even while resting quietly in a chair.
It is constant throughout the day and never completely lets up, and I have never experienced anything like this before.
It feels much harder to breathe when I lie flat on my back, so I have to prop myself up with three pillows to sleep.
Any slight movement makes it worse, but leaning forward while sitting up gives me a little bit of relief.
No, I haven't heard any wheezing or whistling sounds when I breathe.
I don't have a cough, no phlegm, and I haven't had any fever or chills.
I feel a heavy, dull ache and tightness across the center of my chest, but it's not a sharp stabbing pain.
My heart feels like it's racing fast in my chest, and I feel very lightheaded whenever I try to stand up, though I haven't passed out.
No, I have not coughed up any blood at all.
My lower legs and ankles have looked a bit puffy over the last couple of days, but I haven't noticed any sudden weight gain.
Neither leg is painful or swollen more than the other, and I haven't had recent surgery, long flights, or taken any hormones.
I feel completely exhausted and drained of energy, but my stools are normal brown and I have had no unusual bleeding.
I feel anxious because it's hard to breathe, but I don't have any tingling or numbness around my mouth or fingers.
I have never had any heart attacks, asthma, or chronic lung problems, and I don't use any inhalers.
I work in an office and haven't been exposed to dust, asbestos, birds, or mold.
I don't take any blood pressure pills, pain relievers, chemotherapy, or heart rhythm drugs.
About two weeks ago I had a mild cold with a slight scratchy throat, but it cleared up on its own after a few days.
My neck veins are so swollen and I feel so lightheaded that I thought my heart might be failing and backing up fluid.
I'm really scared that my heart is just going to give out and stop while I'm at home alone.
I hope you can do an ultrasound of my heart today and give me something to get my blood pressure back up.
My past medical history is unremarkable, with no high blood pressure, diabetes, or kidney trouble.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only have an occasional glass of wine socially once or twice a month.
I work as an office manager and live with my husband in an apartment.
There is no family history of early heart disease, blood clots, or sudden unexpected deaths.
I went through menopause naturally five years ago, and I have not had any bleeding since.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 88/58 mmHg, heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 95% on room air; pulsus paradoxus noted with an inspiratory systolic drop greater than 10 mmHg.
Patient appears fatigued, anxious, and mildly tachypneic, sitting upright and leaning slightly forward; no central or peripheral cyanosis or digital clubbing.
Marked jugular venous distension extending above the angle of the jaw at 45 degrees, with prominent venous pulsations.
Distant, muffled heart sounds with sinus tachycardia; no murmurs, gallops, or audible friction rub.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields without wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Resonant percussion note bilaterally throughout both lung fields.
Chest expansion is symmetric without chest wall tenderness; apical impulse is faint and difficult to palpate.
Radial pulses are rapid, weak, and thready, with a noticeable decrease in pulse volume during inspiration.
Mild bilateral trace pretibial pitting edema without skin induration or stasis changes.
Calves are symmetric and supple without unilateral swelling, warmth, erythema, or tenderness on palpation.
Abdomen is soft, flat, and non-tender without guarding, rigidity, or palpable hepatosplenomegaly.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are anicteric.
